    A QUIET MORNING IN THE VILLAGE

    CHAPTER I

It was a bright morning in the village, and the baker had opened
his shutters to look out upon the empty street. He whistled while
he worked, and a smell of new bread drifted across the square
where the children played beneath the chestnut trees.

“Good morning to you,” said the baker, leaning upon his counter
with both elbows. “You are about early, and the sun is hardly up
above the roof of the mill.”

“I could not sleep,” the young woman answered him. “There was a
great noise down in the harbour all night long, and I lay awake
and listened to it until the dawn came.”

The baker nodded slowly. He had heard the noise himself, though
he had said nothing of it to his wife, who slept as soundly as a
stone and would not thank him for waking her.

Down at the harbour the fishing boats were coming in, and their
brown sails hung slack in the still air. Three men stood on the
quay and argued about a rope, while a fourth sat apart and mended
a net that had been torn in the night.

“They will be talking of it for a month,” the woman said. “Such a
thing has not happened here within my memory, nor within my
mother’s memory before me.”

She took her loaf and went out into the sunlight, and the baker
watched her cross the square and turn the corner by the church
before he returned to his ovens and his work.
